posts.title: For the Democrats, now comes the hard part
posts.author: Noah Smith
posts.description: The Dems have to figure out what they stand for, and what they want to do.
posts.summary_text: Noah Smith argues that Democrats' sweeping 2026 midterm victory is an opportunity rather than a durable mandate. He compares it with post-Watergate wins that did not prevent a subsequent Republican resurgence. With Congress but not the presidency, Democrats can block damaging policies, investigate alleged corruption, and explain what they would do if elected in 2028. Smith says opposition to Trump cannot substitute for a coherent governing vision. He critiques three possible intellectual leaders: the socialist left, Warren-style progressives focused on attacking wealthy technology firms, and the Abundance movement, which he regards as the most promising but insufficient on its own. He favors practical reforms, material prosperity, and an inclusive sense of national purpose. He also sees fiscal tradeoffs and preparations for AI-related labor disruption as tests of whether Democrats can build a credible policy agenda.

posts.title: Normal Americans punished MAGA
posts.author: Noah Smith
posts.description: Normies exist, and there’s only so far you can push them before they get mad.
posts.summary_text: Writing after the 2026 US midterm elections, Noah Smith interprets the Democratic wave as a rejection of Donald Trump's leadership rather than an embrace of the ideological left. He argues that Republican activists underestimated ordinary swing voters and put too much faith in online partisan narratives and supposedly hidden Trump supporters. In his account, concerns about living costs, government corruption, and perceived mismanagement drove voters away from the GOP, including groups that had previously supported it. Smith points to Democratic gains in traditionally Republican states as evidence that political loyalties can shift dramatically. But he warns Democrats not to mistake this victory for a mandate for unpopular cultural positions, sweeping spending commitments, or rigid left-wing economic policies. His broader argument is that governing competence and responsiveness to mainstream priorities matter more than social-media enthusiasm.

posts.title: Anthropic’s moat is Claude
posts.author: Noah Smith
posts.description: The bull case for Anthropic’s IPO.
posts.summary_text: Smith examines whether Anthropic's reported valuation can be justified by its future competitive position. Spectacular recent revenue growth and strong enterprise interest do not, in his view, guarantee attractive long-term investment returns, especially when the starting valuation is already enormous. The central question is whether Anthropic can establish a durable competitive advantage that lets it retain profits rather than lose them through price competition. Conventional defenses such as network effects, switching costs, and brand loyalty appear weaker in AI than in established consumer software. Smith contrasts this possibility with commodity-like industries, where valuable products can still produce thin margins. In the publicly accessible portion, he raises an unusual hypothesis: superior intelligence itself could allow an AI company to outcompete rivals persistently. The article continues beyond the available preview, so this proposition should be understood as a possibility rather than a demonstrated conclusion.

posts.title: Where’s the “intelligence explosion”?
posts.author: Ramez Naam
posts.description: Art by GPT-6 One of my fundamental beliefs about the world is that Ramez Naam ought to blog more. Ramez is one of the world’s greatest futurists — he predicted the solar and battery revolutions long before these were widely understood. If you were reading Ramez in 2011, you were able to understand the future of both energy technology and climate change, long before other people did. His earlier book More than Human is still a great guide to the kind of biological enhancements that AI might make possible.
